_about: The war plan (after release 1; off by default, and off the game is release 1's move for move). A computer staff that thinks a season ahead. Month by month a staff weighs each front and attacks where the whole front's strength ratio is good enough (open.json). That leaves three gaps a thoughtful commander would not: a front at even strength sleeps for years because nobody gathers the army at one place; an enemy foothold on the coast is watched and never thrown back; and reserves answer only the enemy standing next door. With 'on' true, at the dial's 'stops' (the two where anything goes: at stop 3, in 24 wars with every staff planning, Germany fell a middle of four months sooner, which par at that stop does not allow until the design director rules on it), the staffs named in 'staffs' (empty: every computer-run nation with a staff character) plan campaigns. 'campaign': when the staff has attacked 'few' times or fewer in 'quiet' months on a front (a front gone quiet), a front whose ratio is at least 'ratio'[0] (under it the staff is on the strategic defensive) and under 'ratio'[1] (over it the ordinary offensive does the work), a staff that leads there (it has 'least' corps of its own fit to mass on the front, and they are the share 'own' or more of all its side has on it: a small ally on a greater army's front makes no plan of its own) picks the enemy province where the force it could gather (the best corps the roads into it can carry, tanks and guns first, from 'reach' marches around) would go in at 'strike' odds or better by the staff's own sums, weighing the road beyond it ('road' for the first province of the easiest road to his capital, 'beside' for its neighbours, less the going and 'works' for fortifications). It spends 'prep' months ([fewest, most]) massing: 'tanks' fast corps and infantry up to 'doors' at each of up to 'most' provinces next to the target, the rest of the line keeping what it needs. When the massed force has 'go' odds at the target by the battle's own reckoning the blow falls and is pressed for 'push' months whatever the front's ratio, as a general offensive along the road that starts where the army stands; if 'prep'[1] months pass without those odds the plan is dropped. After a campaign the front rests 'rest' months. 'foothold': an enemy piece of ground of 'size' provinces or fewer on this staff's own side's ground, with the sea behind it, is thrown back before it grows: where the staff's own sums give the force it can bring 'go' odds, and no other front with a real army on it stands under the ratio 'safe', it masses against it at once, whatever else it is doing ('tanks' fast corps and infantry up to 'doors' at each of up to 'most' provinces beside it), strikes at 'go' odds and presses for 'push' months; it keeps at it while the foothold has 'grown' provinces or fewer, after which it is a front like any other. 'recall' (its own 'on' is false: built, measured and left off. In 24 wars with it Italy left the war a middle of four months later than without, and Germany fell no sooner: the corps called out of Africa, home or to the camp of the army abroad on the island it had just taken, were the ones whose next steps, Crete and then Sardinia or Sicily, put Italy out; and the home army was never short of men for France, only of a place to put them ashore. It waits for the design director's form of 'the need ends and the corps go where the next need is'): an army that has won its theatre goes back into the war. An army standing on friendly ground across the water, in one piece away from home, with no enemy on that ground or next to it (nor an enemy's ally, at war yet or not: Italy in Libya in 1939) and no battle on it or beside it for 'quiet' months, keeps a guard (one corps for each harbour of that ground an enemy's troopships can still reach, no fewer than 'least' (nor than a landing force, open.json 'descent.force', so that the ground stays a quay its army abroad can name for its next step) and no more than 'most', the weakest of them; the corps an order holds in place stay besides, and so does the landing force of the army abroad: the corps at its quay and, where 'landing.waves' is set, the waves it counts on, the best within those marches of the quay, as many as a first wave and the ships' months after it; and nobody is called from the homeland across a strait) and sends the rest, the strongest first, with the shipping left after the month's landings: into a harbour of a front its side holds across the water (its own landing first), where the test of strength lets a corps in; or home, to the landing quay; over no crossing riskier than 'risk', and from the harbours of Egypt round the Cape where the Mediterranean is too dangerous, the way they came (middle-east.json). While the army abroad's landing force is short of that count, the corps sent gather to it first: by sea into a harbour within those marches of its quay, or by road to the quay where the roads join. Those not in a harbour march to the nearest one with a way out. Not for a staff whose army goes by the ocean runs. 'landing': with 'second' true, a staff whose men ashore are still too few but whose every harbour there is full, so that no ship can bring another corps, lands its next wave on a harbour beside the ground they hold, that month, with no wait and no dice, under every test of a landing; where before it waited. 'waves': a planning staff reckons an invasion as a campaign, in place of the test of strength as ruled (open.json 'descent.strength'), on the same count of strength and against the same chance. The test as ruled counts one place and what five corps can hold there, so a staff with twenty corps free at home waited until five would do. A planning staff counts, behind a first wave as big as its ships lift (the quay is filled for it), the waves that follow in the months that are left: its fit corps free on quiet ground within 'within' marches of the quay, as many as the ships carry in those months and the floor at home lets go, at 'share' of their strength (not every wave finds room ashore on its day), where the place has another harbour of an enemy's beside it to land them on. And it counts the enemy's reply: his reserves out of the line 'reply' times over, for a staff that plans rails all it has free to a foothold at once ('foothold'). It feeds a foothold on the same reckoning it landed on; and while its men ashore are too few, the quay it feeds them from draws 'tanks' of its fast corps at a time as well as infantry (a foothold breaks out with tanks). And it builds the ships for it: with a landing in view and an army waiting on ships (more of the corps it counts on for its waves than its shipping, built and building, lifts in a month), it lays down troopships from the arsenal, one lot a month, at the player's price and above its reserve, within what the yards can take (arsenal.json 'lift'), until its shipping lifts 'ships' corps a month (two harbours' worth). Before, no computer staff ever laid one down. 'ops' (the staff's own operations: the great choices on its menu, open.json 'ops'; from the playtester's traces of 22 November 2026). They have a switch of their own, 'ops.on', off, and their own stops, which take in stop 3 where par is read: off, the game is release 1's move for move. 'keep': a staff keeps the force of an operation it still means to launch. The corps its landings name stand held at their ports whatever offensive opens beside them (before, the offensive in the west took three of the four groups meant for Norway from Bremen, and one corps sailed); and ground of its own beside a country the operation would declare war on is no idle ground, so the desk for its army abroad leaves the garrison there (before, Italy's desk took the whole garrison of Albania for a landing on Cyprus, Italy then declared war on Greece with nobody in Albania, and the Greek army walked in). 'port': the harbour of a foothold is not left empty. On a piece of friendly ground away from the staff's homeland of 'size' provinces or fewer, a harbour with an enemy field corps within 'within' marches keeps one corps of the staff's on it for the month, the one that adds least to an attack (before, the one German corps ashore at Oslo marched inland, a Norwegian division walked into the harbour behind it, and the corps died cut off). 'front': an operation's landing is its staff's second front from the day. The landing desk names an enemy only after a year of quiet war with him (open.json 'descent.after'), so nobody fed the corps an operation put ashore, and a landing that failed was tried again a year on. A planning staff's home desk takes the enemy its operation declared on for its own the month the operation goes, and the first harbour the operation takes is its lodgment: fed through that harbour while the men ashore are fewer than 'descent.feed' times the enemy next to their ground (a side-show is not built up to a second front's fifteen divisions), widened where it is full, and landed on again under the desk's own tests where the operation was beaten off. 'home': the army of an operation that is won goes home. Once the country the operation landed on has fallen, the staff keeps on that ground the corps its orders hold there and the weakest of the rest, until those kept come to 'guard' divisions or to 'descent.feed' times the enemy on that ground and next to it, and the others take ship for a home harbour as the ships lift them, over no crossing riskier than 'risk' (before, the eight corps that took Norway by November 1940 in one war stood there when the attack on the Soviet Union opened; over 24 wars Germany had three to five corps fewer on its eastern front and fell 3.3 months sooner). 'held' and 'reach' are the guard as ruled on 22 November 2026 (19:36Z): the corps the guard keeps are held where they stand for the month (before, they were free and the main staff marched them away: seed 19, the 18 divisions in Norway all went east through Finland in two months), and the enemy it reckons with is every enemy corps the staff can see that could strike that ground within a month's march, by the reach the player is shown, in place of those on the ground and next to it; there is no ceiling, since the guard only keeps and never calls corps in. 'watch' (the same ruling) is the coast watch on every coast a side holds: each country's coast is a watch of its own, the homeland's and each conquered country's (a country that has fallen: while it still fights, the harbours taken from it are a front's and are not watched), a corps a harbour (open.json 'coast.each'), the most valuable first, up to the sum of the sea lift of every enemy whose ships reach that coast, and never more than the harbours held; open.json's 'coast.share' and 'coast.least' are not read (the size comes from the cause). A coast's watch is found by land from the corps on that ground, and on the ground of an operation that is won the guard counts the watch's corps as kept and sends none of them home. A side's own harbours overseas are not watched, as before. A corps kept back from an offensive's release for an operation that then went without it is released the month the staff no longer keeps it. 'lead': an operation is meant, and its force kept, from this many months before its first month. 'landing' (the design director's ruling of 22 November 2026, in a general form for every nation and theatre; its own switch 'landing.on', off, read only where 'ops.on' is on). Built, measured and left off. In 24 wars at stop 3 no build of it brought the landing on Sicily (none by July 1943; Sardinia stays the first Italian shore landed on), and with 'quay' and 'defer' on Italy left the war 2.5 months later than with the operations alone (se 1.4) and six wars of 24 saw no landing on Italy's home ground at all: the quay rule drew a desk's army forward in a packet of three corps (America's from Cornwall to Gibraltar and on to Tripoli by December 1942, in one war) to a quay it could not be reinforced through, where it had neither the odds nor a safe crossing. Those two are false here; with them false the rest moves Italy's month by +0.9 (se 1.1). What bars Sicily is the test of strength (open.json 'descent.strength'), which none of these rules touches: Sicily is one province a march from the mainland, so the reckoning sets Italy's home army against the five corps one province holds (Britain's army at Tripoli, August 1943, one war: a chance of 0.35 where 0.6 is asked; Sardinia, with no land beside it, 0.90). It waits for the design director's ruling. 'quay': the beach is chosen first, among the harbours within a landing's range of any quay the desk's army could sail from, and the quay is the one with a crossing open to its troopships this month and no riskier than a staff takes, then the one fewest seas from the beach; the desk moves its force there. 'defer' and 'allies': a desk leaves a beach to a nearer army of its own staff's, or of an ally's, that has named a beach of the same enemy's and could sail this month, for 'patience' months from the month that army named its beach. 'wave': the first wave is the smallest of the corps ready at the quay, from the usual force to as many as the ships lift, that has the odds on the beach and is not outnumbered next door; where none has and the ships could lift more than stand ready, the quay is filled. 'wait': a beach the desk has named that only the sky, a closed sea or the march to its quay bars this month is waited for, for the half year a beach stays named, and nothing is spent on a lesser beach meanwhile; the fighters fight for that sky as before, and with 'fleet' the staff's free fleets within reach count together toward opening a sea on a named crossing that no one of them could open alone. 'beyond': a beach is worth more for what lies inland of it, the towns, works and capital within 'marches' of it over enemy ground, each divided by its marches, times 'share'. 'torch' (Operation Torch by the book: the design director's rulings of 22 November 2026, on the historian's rows; its own switch, 'torch.on', off, and off the game is release 1's move for move). In the grand campaign no staff ever went to war with Vichy: French North Africa stayed at peace, the roster's Tunisian rows never came, Italy fought 1943 with its heart whole and the record's quays for Sicily were nobody's. With the switch on, at its 'stops' of the history dial (the two that keep the book) and while the book stands on the second front, Britain's and America's staffs have the operation of November 1942 on their menus ('ops': the entries of open.json that history.json lists under 'bookOnly' and dates; they are on no staff's menu anywhere else): the declaration on Vichy, and the landings at Casablanca, Oran and Algiers. By the book a landing goes where the record's went, the first shore its entry names, and on its day whatever the odds: the fight is the few days the French resisted, and the French turn follows at the month's end. ('ceasefire', a key of its own that ships off: at the turn a force the French threw back on the day goes ashore at that shore if the turn gave the place to its side, with no lift and no second crossing reckoned. The design director struck it on 22 November 2026, since it hides a throw-back the record never had; it is kept only so that the wars read with it can be run again.) After the day it is that shore still, but not against the odds. The other shores an entry lists are for a staff that chooses for itself. Britain's landing is the roster's dated row (the 78th Division, at Gibraltar, or at a home quay within reach where Gibraltar is full). America's are made from its own corps, with no new men (a landing entry with 'own', the worth the record sent: the corps of its own, standing at a harbour its side holds within a landing's reach of the beach, that is nearest to it in size; it is kept at its quay from 'lead' months before the day, and one out of reach is shipped to the operation's 'quay', Gibraltar, as the ships and the room allow). 'turn' is the French turn: that event (diplomacy.json) is tried at the end of the landing's own month as well as when the next one opens, its partition runs as the record wrote it (the test that an heir must stand on Vichy's home ground is set aside), the Axis divisions it raises are left out, and the roster's dated rows come instead (setup-1939.json 'torch': Nehring's first wave, the 334th, the Hermann Goring and the rest by their months; the French who came over as XIX Corps, made from the Army of Africa and never added to it, formed at the turn itself where the largest of that army stood, so that the ports it held are not left empty). 'week' (the design director, 22 November 2026, 13:27Z): the week of the landing's month in which the book's turn falls. The record's ceasefire came on the third day, so at these stops the turn is tried right after the landings, in their own week, once every nation of the operation has made its landings that month, whoever then holds the shores (a month in which only one of them landed keeps the month's end). A landing's fight is cut short by it: both sides lose that many quarters of the month's toll in men (the game's month is four weeks), and a force whose fight was not decided goes ashore where it landed when the turn gives the place to its side. 0: the turn at the month's end and the fight a month's, as it was read before. Stops 3 to 5 are unchanged: whether a staff of its own accord fights Vichy is another ruling. 'fronts' (the design director, 22 November 2026, 13:27Z; a key of its own, and with it off nothing is read. ON in release 2's rules: the design director ruled it on at 17:59Z the same day, once its 96 wars at stop 3 held every mark of the gate (war-plan/gate-fronts-month-96.txt), and Brian chose 'Switch it on for release 2' at 18:01Z. The tilt is recorded, not tuned: about 7 wars in 96 toward the Soviet Union and the middle war a month earlier): the one-map fault. A staff's sum for a front counted every corps of its side standing anywhere on the friendly land that touches it, however far: Rommel's army at El Alamein was counted into an attack out of Tunis, 8 to 13 marches away. With 'month' on, in the grand campaign, every staff's front counts only what the month's moves can bring to it: a corps that can march to a province on the front within its month (the roads' weeks, staff.ts monthReach) or be carried there by train (the walk the railway makes, game.ts railInto; no trains in the desert). What a front must leave for the others is reckoned the same way: another front's need is met first by the corps only it can reach, and only what is left is taken from the corps both can reach. The works, the garrisons and the enemy's side of the sum are as they were. 'straits' (the design director, 22 November 2026, 09:20Z; a key of its own, off): every short crossing of the sea on the chart is water, for every nation, in the grand campaign. A corps crosses to a bank its side holds by ship: it takes its whole month, one of its nation's lifts and room on the far bank, and the crossing carries its own quays (no harbour is asked on either bank). A side that holds both banks crosses whoever holds the seas beyond, and the convoy may still be found. An attack across onto an enemy bank is a landing: the corps that cross fight at the landing's share of their strength, each on a lift, and they cross only where a sea the two banks share is open to their troopships and the enemy's fighters do not hold the sky (the month war is declared, neither is asked). Supply and the railways run over a crossing as before. The landing desk's test of strength (ashore.ts) counts the corps of either side beyond a crossing by what can be brought over in its months, as it counts its own follow-up, and no longer in full (the enemy's by the ruling of 09:20Z, the force's own friends by that of 18:07Z: one rule serves both sides). The rulings of 18:07Z and 18:19Z, with the historian's rows (historian/short-crossings-1939-45.md, historian/straits-craft-and-sea-lift-1122.md; worth 1.0 is 15,000 men): 'craft' is what a crossing's own craft carry in a month to a bank the side holds, in divisions' worth, the record's busiest month there, for whoever holds the bank: Messina 7 (August 1943), Kerch 17 (the Kuban evacuation of September and October 1943), the Oresund 3.7 (Germany's leave traffic through Sweden), the Great Belt 2.75 (ruled 18:26Z: the middle of the 2.5 to 3 divisions a month of the Danish State Railways' measured working of the Little Belt ferries next door; the Great Belt's own 7 to 15 is a ceiling with no timetable or weather in it and is not laid). A corps the craft have room for crosses with no lift; one they have no room for goes by its nation's shipping. The Bosporus, the Dardanelles, Vancouver, Canso and the two southern crossings have no month on the record and no figure here: they read the side's sea lift alone. 'lift' is the record's sea lift in corps a month for a nation whose sealift is a stand-in, read at the crossings (on the seas named, where any are): Germany 5 in April 1940 (four in Norway and one in Denmark, so the one over its sealift is the crossings' own and takes nothing from Norway's four), the Soviet Union 2 in the Black Sea and Azov (Kerch and Feodosia in December 1941, Kerch and Eltigen in November 1943), France 1 (Norway 1940); Turkey, Denmark and Sweden landed no force and have none. 'more' names borders of the chart that are crossings too (Istanbul to Izmir: the Dardanelles) and 'cut' borders that are open sea (Jutland to Gothenburg: the Kattegat). Supply and the railways run over a crossing as before; over a cut border nothing runs (ruled 18:29Z: cut means cut): no army but by a landing, no supply and no train. 'bridges' are dated rows: the crossing is a land link in those months while the country named holds both banks and has held them since the month given (the Kerch railway bridge, November 1944 to February 1945, both banks Soviet since May 1944). With the key off none of this is read and the chart is as it was.
